phases.name: Production readiness — wrong-verdict closure and operational hardening
phases.weeks: 11d (after phase-dd, still ahead of the phase-4 launch surfaces)
phases.ships: Fourteen gaps between the built binary and production, seven of them REPRODUCED WRONG VERDICTS on a live PostgreSQL 16 — a migration that Postgres rejects outright returning PASS with exit 0. Plus one that stops `validate` running at all on any schema using an extension type (citext, hstore, pgvector, postgis), an empty-table false FAIL, a verdict contract that reports FAIL with no finding and no remediation, a fixture-size budget guarded only by a synthetic input, a `pull` with no timeouts to point at production, and a lint job that cannot start.
phases.source: Deep-dive session: a local PostgreSQL 16.13 cluster (Docker-free initdb recipe), driven end to end through pull -> hydrate -> validate against a schema built from what production schemas actually contain and the corpus does not — identity and STORED generated columns, a range-partitioned parent with two partitions, a covering UNIQUE index with INCLUDE, an extension type (citext) and a trigram opclass index, CHECK constraints, a self-referencing FK with ON DELETE CASCADE, mixed-case quoted identifiers, an unlogged zero-row table, a materialized view, RLS, triggers — plus a 300-table schema for the size budget. Each defect was confirmed by running the SAME statement against the source database and comparing what Postgres did to what rowshape said.
phases.scope_note: Placed after phase-dd and still BEFORE the phase-4 launch, for the same reason phase-cr and phase-dd are: these are defects in the code the launch demos. THE PATTERN IS THE SAME ONE PHASE-DD NAMED, one level deeper. phase-dd drove real Postgres and caught the fixtures pull could not hydrate. This dive asked the next question — when hydration SUCCEEDS, is the disposable database actually equivalent to production? It is not. Seven facts production enforces (CHECK, FK, INCLUDE-key separation, generated columns, partitioning, exact extremes, empty tables) never reach the target, and every one of them was demonstrated to produce a verdict that disagrees with what the source database does. Six of the seven are WRONG PASSES, which INV-CONFIDENCE-CAPPING calls the one thing that must never be wrong: an agent gets PASS, opens the PR, and the migration fails in production. The unit tests and the 28-case corpus are all blind to this because they assert the verdict a fixture implies, never the verdict the SOURCE DATABASE would give.
phases.definition_of_done: For every gap below, the same statement run against the source database and against rowshape agrees. A schema using extension types hydrates. A migration that Postgres rejects never returns PASS. A migration that fails to apply returns a finding with remediation, not an empty findings list. `pull` is safe to point at a production primary. Full suite green with ROWSHAPE_TEST_PG_DSN set, and scripts/verify-all.sh reports no failures.

tasks.found_by_deep_dive: A `citext` email column — the single most common reason a real Postgres schema depends on an extension. `pull` recorded the column as `type: citext` and nothing recorded that citext comes from an extension, so hydrate aborted the whole DDL transaction: `ddl failed: ERROR: type "citext" does not exist (SQLSTATE 42704)`, exit 3. Same failure shape for hstore, ltree, postgis geometry, and pgvector's `vector` — which is now in a large share of new schemas. On any such schema rowshape delivers nothing at all. The related half showed up one layer down: with citext swapped for text the load succeeded but `CREATE INDEX "orders_email_trgm" ON "app"."orders" USING gin ("email")` failed with `data type text has no default operator class for access method "gin"`, because the recorded index lost its `gin_trgm_ops` opclass. `orders_paid_idx` lost `DESC NULLS LAST` the same way.
tasks.title: An extension type stops `validate` running at all
tasks.description: The fixture records nothing about extensions, so a fresh disposable database — which has none installed beyond plpgsql — cannot be told to install them. Add an `extensions` block to the fixture (spec-additive, alongside §6.7 user-defined types) listing the extensions the read schema actually depends on: read pg_extension joined to what the in-scope columns, index opclasses, and type namespaces reference, so an unused extension is not carried. `target.DDL` emits `CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS <name>` — with an explicit schema where the source has one — before CREATE TYPE and CREATE TABLE. An extension the disposable server does not have available must fail LOUDLY and name it (the operator can install it or use a different image); it must not silently degrade the type to text, because a citext column is case-insensitive and a text one is not, which is itself a wrong-verdict source. Separately, index keys must keep their opclass and ordering: `pull` already emits `keys` verbatim from pg_get_indexdef for EXPRESSION indexes (DD phase), but a plain-column index goes through `columns` and loses both. Record the per-key opclass/collation/ordering, or emit `keys` for any index whose definition is not reconstructible from bare column names.

Verified end to end against PostgreSQL 16.13. A schema with citext (plain and citext[]) columns, a `gin (email gin_trgm_ops)` index, a `(created_at DESC NULLS LAST)` partial index and a `UNIQUE (customer_id, created_at) INCLUDE (total)` covering index now pulls, hydrates and reproduces itself: `diff` of `indexdef` for every index in the schema between source and hydrated target is EMPTY, and the target's columns come back as `citext` / `citext[]` rather than degraded to text. No version is recorded and no degradation to text is attempted — citext is case-insensitive and text is not, so a substitution would convert a loud failure into a wrong verdict. (3) `include` (RFC §6.5): the catalog read splits indkey at indnkeyatts, so a covering index's payload stops widening its key; the explicit Index marshaller had to be taught the field, which is exactly the trap its own comment warns about. (4) The rendered index key is now assembled from indclass/indoption rather than taken from pg_get_indexdef's per-column form. That form returns the key EXPRESSION only — the belief recorded in the old comment that it includes "any DESC or operator class" was wrong, which is why `(seen_at DESC NULLS LAST)` came back as `seen_at` and the trigram index came back unbuildable. Non-default parts only, so an ordinary ascending btree key still renders bare and no existing fixture churns (verified: `payload_gin` on the default jsonb_ops carries no `keys`). (5) RFC §6.8 written, §6.5 extended for `include` and for keys that carry ordering/collation/opclass, and the published JSON Schema updated.

tasks.title: CHECK constraints never reach the disposable database — reproduced wrong PASS
tasks.description: internal/target/ddl.go's header says CHECK expressions are "intentionally NOT emitted here" because "a CHECK can carry domain logic that obviously-fake values needn't satisfy", and defers reintroducing them to "`validate` (phase 2)". Phase 2 shipped and nothing in internal/validate reintroduces them — grep for ADD CONSTRAINT across the package returns nothing. So the deferral became a permanent hole, and it is the ordinary case, not an exotic one: nearly every production table has a CHECK. The stated worry is real but has the wrong remedy. Emit recorded CHECKs, but AFTER the rows are loaded and as a separate, individually-reported step in the same shape SecondaryIndexes already uses: a savepoint per constraint, so a CHECK that synthesized data cannot satisfy is REPORTED as a constraint the disposable database is not enforcing, rather than silently dropped (today's behavior) or aborting the load (the feared behavior). That distinction is the whole point — an unenforced constraint the operator was told about is a known limit; one nobody was told about is a wrong PASS. A `privacy: strict` `opaque` expression is skipped, exactly as createType already skips an opaque domain CHECK.

A CHECK that hydrated data cannot satisfy is reported on stderr naming the constraint, and the run continues — it is neither silently dropped nor fatal.

tasks.verified:
Verified end to end against PostgreSQL 16.13. The reproduced wrong PASS is closed: `UPDATE app.orders SET status = 'archived' WHERE status = 'shipped'` against a table carrying `CHECK (status IN ('pending','paid','shipped'))` now returns FAIL with exit 1, matching the source database's `ERROR: new row for relation "orders" violates check constraint "orders_status_chk"`. Before this it returned PASS with exit 0. A migration that respects the constraint (`SET status = 'paid'`) still returns PASS, so the fix did not simply make everything fail. `pg_constraint` for the hydrated target now matches the source on every CHECK.

Two halves, and only together do they close it. (1) target.DeferredConstraints renders ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK, applied after the rows, each inside its own savepoint via a new shared execGuarded helper (SecondaryIndexes now uses it too). Failures land in LoadReport.SkippedConstraints and both `hydrate` and `validate` print them: a constraint the target does not enforce is never silent again. NOT VALID is preserved — recreating such a constraint as validated would make the target reject data production holds, and would leave a migration's own VALIDATE CONSTRAINT nothing to validate. `opaque` (privacy:strict) is skipped rather than invented, matching what createType already does for an opaque domain CHECK.

(2) The savepoint alone would have left the wrong PASS open, because the synthesis engine could not satisfy the constraint — the first run reported `check constraint "orders_status_chk" is violated by some row` and skipped it. The original objection recorded in ddl.go ("a CHECK can carry domain logic that obviously-fake values needn't satisfy") was real; the remedy was wrong. internal/hydrate/checkdomain.go now reads a table's CHECKs the same way the engine already reads an enum's labels: a column under `CHECK (status IN (...))` is an enum in all but name. It extracts a literal value set (`= ANY (ARRAY[...])`, which is how Postgres renders IN) or inclusive numeric bounds, intersecting multiple CHECKs and splitting top-level AND. Values replace; bounds clamp, so a column keeps the recorded distribution wherever it already satisfies the bound. NULLs are never touched (a CHECK is satisfied by NULL, and the null fraction is a recorded fact) — pinned by a test. Synthesized statuses now come back as the real pending/paid/shipped vocabulary, which is drawn from the CHECK expression the fixture already publishes verbatim at `standard` (§6.4), so no new information leaves the source.

It is deliberately NOT a SQL evaluator. Multi-column comparisons, function calls, disjunctions, single-value equality (which would collapse the recorded cardinality), and NOT VALID constraints (obeying one would make the target STRICTER than production) all yield no domain — generation is unchanged and the constraint is reported as skipped. Six negative cases pin that, and they are the load-bearing ones: a guess here would constrain hydrated data in a way production does not.

Tests: four in internal/target/check_ddl_test.go (CHECKs emitted; inline kinds not re-added; opaque not reconstructed; NOT VALID preserved and not applied to validated constraints) and seven in internal/hydrate/checkdomain_test.go (three membership spellings incl. the `(status)::text` cast form; bounds with strict comparisons nudged inside; conjunction splitting; the six-case negative table; NOT VALID ignored; end-to-end generation satisfying both a set and bounds without collapsing cardinality; null fraction preserved). Full `go test ./...` green with ROWSHAPE_TEST_PG_DSN set, including the 28-case corpus and the demo regression; gofmt and go vet clean.

tasks.title: `validate` can hang forever applying a migration that is an outage
tasks.description:
internal/validate/capture.go executes each migration statement with no statement_timeout, so a statement that would be an outage in production is an outage in the disposable database — `validate` blocks until the statement finishes, the context is cancelled, or someone kills it. That was survivable only while the target under-enforced: with foreign keys dropped (PR-T3) the cascade never happened, so the run was fast for the wrong reason.

The fix is not to stop reproducing the hazard — reproducing it is the product. It is that `validate` must not have to SURVIVE an outage to REPORT one. Cap the apply with a `SET statement_timeout`, exposed as a flag with a documented default, and treat a cancellation (SQLSTATE 57014) as EVIDENCE rather than as a failure: the statement did not complete within the ceiling, so its duration is `>= ceiling`, which is precisely what the `outage` bucket in INV-DURATIONS-BUCKETS means. It is emphatically NOT a tool error (the tool worked) and NOT a clean apply failure (nothing was rejected) — and it can never license a PASS, because a statement that did not finish has not been shown to be safe.
acceptance_criteria: A migration statement that exceeds the ceiling is cancelled, and `validate` returns rather than blocking.
A cancelled statement can never produce PASS; the verdict is at least WARN.
A cancellation is distinguished from a rejected statement (a real FAIL) and from a tool error (exit 3).
The ceiling is a flag with a documented default, and disabling it requires an explicit opt-in.
The `cascade_delete_fanout` corpus case still reports WARN — the timeout adds evidence and does not overturn the expected verdict.
The full suite completes well inside the Go test timeout with foreign keys enforced.

tasks.verified:
Verified end to end against PostgreSQL 16.13. The `cascade_delete_fanout` corpus case — which had turned a 190-second suite into a 10-minute hard timeout the moment PR-T3 made the target enforce real foreign keys — now returns WARN with RS-PERF-001 in 98 seconds. The expected verdict was PRESERVED, not relaxed: the timeout adds evidence and does not overturn the analyzer's conclusion. The three slow suites (test/action, test/demo, corpus/harness) complete in 4m00s together.

The hazard was never the bug. Reproducing it is the product: that DELETE matches 244,223 parent rows, each cascading into a 10,000,000-row child table with no index on the referencing column, because the fixture records none — production has none. Postgres seq-scans 10M rows per deleted parent. The bug was that `validate` had to SURVIVE the outage in order to REPORT it.

`ApplyWithTimeout` sets a session `statement_timeout` (default 60s, `--statement-timeout`, `0` disables it as a deliberate opt-in). Session-level rather than per-statement so it also covers CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which runs outside a transaction, and so a migration's own explicit SET can still override it. A server that refuses the SET does not stop the run; it stops rowshape claiming a ceiling is in force.

The load-bearing decision is that a cancellation is a THIRD outcome, not a flavour of failure (recorded as D-019). A rejected statement is a real FAIL — the data or the schema said no. A cancelled one said nothing at all: it did not finish, which is evidence its duration is at least the ceiling — precisely what the `outage` bucket means (INV-DURATIONS-BUCKETS). So `Capture.TimedOut` is kept separate from `Capture.Success`, and the statement's SQLSTATE 57014 is CLEARED rather than carried, because leaving it would report an outage as though a constraint had been violated. The verdict floors to WARN: FAIL would assert a defect nobody observed, PASS would certify a statement that never completed — the same rule INV-CONFIDENCE-CAPPING states for weak facts, applied to an absent observation.

Sixty seconds is chosen against what the number is used for, not against how long a real migration takes: hydrated data is a fraction of production and `validate` runs inside an agent's turn, so a statement still running after a minute there is already decisively in the slow/outage buckets.

Tests: six in internal/validate/timeout_test.go — a timed-out capture cannot PASS and floors to WARN; a clean capture still PASSes (the floor must not fire spuriously); a REJECTED statement still FAILs (collapsing the two would downgrade every real failure); a live pg_sleep(30) is cancelled inside 10s with TimedOut set, no SQLSTATE, and Success intact; with the ceiling disabled no timeout is claimed; and fast statements are untouched by the ceiling. Docs: `--statement-timeout` documented in docs/action.md with the WARN floor explained; D-019 records the decision and the table of the three outcomes.

The synthesis engine already assigns FK-consistent values (assignForeignKeys, hydrate/fanout.go), so the constraints should validate; where they do not, the per-constraint savepoint reports it rather than dropping it. Before this it returned PASS with exit 0. ddl.go's stated blocker was that "a foreign key needs dependency-ordered loading". It does not, if the constraint is ADDED AFTER the rows rather than declared in CREATE TABLE — which is also what pg_dump does. That makes table load order irrelevant, and it is what makes self-references and cycles work; a test asserts no FOREIGN KEY appears in DDL (which runs before any row exists) and that a two-table cycle yields two constraints.

The fixture gained three fields on Reference: `name`, `on_update`, and `validated`. `name` is the one that matters most and is not cosmetic — a COMPOSITE key is recorded as one entry per column pair so `fanout` stays per-column, and without the shared name a consumer cannot tell `FOREIGN KEY (a, b) REFERENCES t (x, y)` from two independent single-column keys, which constrain different things. addForeignKeys groups by name and preserves column order within each group. NOT VALID is preserved, since validating such a key here would make the target reject data production holds and would leave a migration's own VALIDATE CONSTRAINT nothing to do. An unrecognized referential action renders nothing rather than a guess, and a `to` that is not schema.table.column is skipped rather than pointed somewhere production does not.

Foreign keys go through the same per-constraint savepoint as CHECKs (PR-T2's execGuarded), so one the synthesized data cannot satisfy is REPORTED by `hydrate` and `validate` rather than dropped silently or taking the load down.

tasks.title: A covering index's INCLUDE columns are flattened into its key — reproduced wrong PASS
tasks.description: `pull` reads index columns from the catalog without distinguishing key columns (the first indnkeyatts) from INCLUDE payload columns, so a covering index's payload is emitted as if it were part of the key. Add `include` to §6.5 alongside the `keys` field the DD phase added, have the catalog read split at indnkeyatts, and render `INCLUDE (...)` in createIndex. Count, strategy and skew DESCRIBE a partitioned table; the key is what lets one be REBUILT. Available since PG 10, so no version gate. An unrecognized rendering yields an empty key rather than a mangled one, and the consumer then reports it cannot rebuild the partitioning instead of declaring PARTITION BY over a guess.

(2) createTable emits `PARTITION BY <strategy> (<key>)`, and target.Partitions creates the partitions after the parents and BEFORE any row — a partitioned parent accepts no rows until a partition can hold them, so a COPY into a bare parent fails outright. Bounds deliberately do NOT match production and do not need to: what changes behaviour is the strategy, the count, and the fact that the table is partitioned. HASH reproduces the count exactly through MODULUS/REMAINDER, which covers the key space by construction and needs no knowledge of the values. RANGE and LIST get a single DEFAULT partition, which catches every row whatever the synthesised values are — a row matching no partition takes the whole load down, and range bounds cannot be reconstructed from a fixture (the key column's `range` is itself sampled — PR-T7).

(3) Where the count is not reproduced it is REPORTED (LoadReport.UnreproducedPartitionCount, surfaced by hydrate and validate): "app.events has 2 range partitions in production; the target has 1". Count is not decoration — a DDL statement on a parent takes locks on every partition and index builds scale with how many there are, so a target standing one partition in for ninety understates the lock, the direction that turns a real finding into a clean run.

One consequence had to be handled: Postgres requires every UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY on a partitioned table to contain the partition key and refuses the whole CREATE TABLE otherwise. Production's constraint satisfies that by construction, but the fixture's may not describe it well enough to prove so, and taking the table down is worse than the constraint being reported as unenforced — so constraintFitsPartitionKey skips those, and only those.

Verified end to end against PostgreSQL 16.13, and it resolves D-010 (recorded as D-020).

The reproduced wrong PASS is closed. `ALTER TABLE app.orders ADD CONSTRAINT CHECK (customer_id <= 59950)` against a sampled maximum of 59,920 and a TRUE maximum of 60,000 now returns WARN with RS-CONSTRAINT-010, saying the range was profiled from a sample, that the bound sits above the sampled maximum "which a sample can only understate", and naming `rowshape pull --exact`. This failure runs the OPPOSITE way to the one capping guards, which is why D-010's reasoning ("absent ranks below every level, so it can never license a PASS") looked safe and was not. Capping caps findings that EXIST; a sampled range makes the finding NOT exist, and a missing finding is a PASS nothing downstream can reach. `absent` was protecting the verdict of a finding that was never made.

Two halves, and half one alone would not have closed it because there is no finding for capping to act on.

(1) `Range` gains `confidence` (RFC §6.2), set from whether `sampleClause` actually sampled — `exact` for extremes read over the whole column, `estimated` for a TABLESAMPLE, and forced to exact in `--exact` mode where the whole column is read. Small tables are read whole already, so most fixtures get exact extremes for free and are not penalized; verified live, `app.categories.id` came back `exact` while `app.orders.customer_id` came back `estimated`. `verdict.factConfidence` now resolves `<table>.<col>.range` instead of returning `absent`.

(2) RS-CONSTRAINT-010 reports the ABSENCE of a conflict when it rests on sampled extremes. There is deliberately NO "comfortably outside the range so it must be fine" escape: a sample gives no bound on how far past its extremes the real data lies, so any threshold would be a guess dressed as one — the class of reasoning INV-CONFIDENCE-CAPPING exists to forbid. A sampled minimum can only be too high and a sampled maximum only too low, so every non-violating comparison against a sampled range is inconclusive. My first attempt DID carve out a "safe direction" and the test caught it: `customer_id >= 0` against a sampled minimum of 5 is not safe, because the true minimum can only be LOWER than 5 and may be negative.

Guarded in both directions. An exact range still certifies absence, so a migration whose bound is genuinely ruled out still PASSes (verified live). A sampled range that ALREADY shows a violation stays a FAIL at severity error — the sample is a lower bound on the spread, so a violation it found is proof, not doubt. And a fixture written before the field carries no confidence and is read as `absent`, not `estimated`: the weakest reading for a fact whose provenance is unknown, and it deliberately does not trigger the new warning wholesale.

Before this, `--json` returned `{"verdict":"FAIL","findings":null}` — no code, no location, no remediation — with the engine's message going to STDERR ONLY, which is nowhere in the machine-readable contract.

That broke the wedge directly rather than cosmetically: `rowshape mcp`'s validate_migration tool and the GitHub Action both render the Verdict struct AND NOTHING ELSE, so an agent was told FAIL and handed nothing to act on — exactly the hand-waving the P4-T8 agent-rule harness scores against. INV-VERDICT-STABLE also requires remediation on every error, and this path had none. And it is the most common real failure there is.

THIS ADDS A SEVENTH FINDING NAMESPACE and that is an extension of the public verdict contract, recorded as D-023 for the owner to confirm. The six existing classes all describe a HAZARD in a migration that RAN — a lock it takes, data it breaks on, an index it rebuilds. This one says the migration DID NOT RUN. Folding it into RS-DATA would claim the data rejected a statement that may never have parsed. The extension is additive: existing codes keep their meaning, and what INV-VERDICT-STABLE guarantees is that codes are permanent and namespaced, not that the namespace list is closed.

Implemented as an ANALYZER in internal/findings rather than inside validate, for a hard reason as well as a stylistic one: analyzers already receive the Capture, and internal/findings imports internal/validate, so building it in validate would have closed an import cycle. The first attempt did exactly that and did not compile.

The remediation is written to be USEFUL to an agent rather than generic: it tells the reader how to interpret the SQLSTATE CLASS — 23 means production-shaped DATA refused it (the migration is syntactically fine and the data does not permit it), 42 means the statement does not match the schema it was written against. That is the difference between "rewrite the migration" and "fix the data", which is the decision the agent actually has to make.

It declares NO depends_on: it rests on what the database DID, not on a fixture fact. Declaring one would be false provenance in a DSSE-signed document — the mistake RS-CONSTRAINT-010 made when it borrowed the row count's confidence.

Also: `findings` now marshals as `[]` rather than `null` when empty, so a consumer can iterate without a nil check. A JSON contract that yields null for "none" makes every reader write the same guard and some of them forget.

Verified on all five surfaces: `--json` carries the finding; the human render shows code, `at file:line`, detail, fix and why; `rowshape explain RS-APPLY-001` resolves; a clean PASS returns `findings: []`; and the exit code is 1.

Tests: four in internal/findings/rsapply_test.go (a failure produces a finding with code, severity, remediation, location, SQLSTATE evidence and no false provenance; a clean apply produces nothing; a FAIL with no identifiable statement stays silent rather than inventing one; and a CANCELLED statement is NOT an apply failure — D-019's third outcome, where nothing rejected the migration and reporting one would claim the database refused something it never got to judge) plus one in internal/validate pinning the [] marshalling.

ONE DESIGN POINT WAS ONLY FOUND BY THE CORPUS. The first version emitted RS-APPLY-001 alongside whatever else fired, and five corpus cases went red: `rsconstraint-check-conflict`, `rsdata-notnull-has-nulls`, `set_not_null_fullscan`, `unique_index_cant_build` and `validate_orphans` all FAIL because the DATA rejected the migration, and every one of them already had a specific analyzer explaining it. RS-APPLY-001 is a FLOOR, not an addition: when RS-DATA-001 already says the column contains NULLs, in the column's own terms, with remediation about the NULLs, adding "read the SQLSTATE" alongside it is a second entry for one event that dilutes the actionable advice. The generic finding is now dropped whenever another ERROR finding explains the same failure, and kept when nothing does — which is the typo case it exists for. The suppression cannot live in an analyzer (they run independently and none can see what the others produced) so it happens in BuildResult, where the whole set is known. Only ERROR findings suppress it: a warning about a migration is not an explanation of why it was rejected. Two more tests pin both directions, and the corpus is green again.

tasks.title: `pull` has nothing to stop it hurting the production database it is pointed at
tasks.description: The entire premise is that `pull` runs against production, and `--exact` is documented as taking "minutes to hours". Today a single profiling query against a large table can run unbounded; a long-lived read transaction holds back vacuum on every table it has touched; and an ACCESS SHARE lock acquired behind a queued ALTER TABLE will stall every subsequent query on that table. None of that is hypothetical for the customer this is aimed at — it is the standard reason DBAs refuse to let a new tool near a primary. Set all three timeouts with SET LOCAL inside the read transaction, expose them as flags with documented defaults, and set `application_name` to `rowshape/<version>` so the connection is identifiable. A timeout must DEGRADE rather than abort: the affected fact drops to estimated or absent, the run continues, and the operational warning names the column and the flag that raises the ceiling — silent truncation is already forbidden and the Warn hook exists for exactly this. Document the read-only role and the timeouts on the privacy/install pages, because being able to point at this section is what gets the tool approved.

application_name identifies rowshape and its version on the connection.
A statement that hits the timeout degrades the affected fact and emits a warning naming the column and the flag; `pull` still writes a usable fixture.
No timeout value can be set to unlimited without an explicit opt-in flag.
The docs state what `pull` does to the database it reads, including the locks it takes and the timeouts it sets.

tasks.verified:
Verified against PostgreSQL 16.13. `application_name` now reads `rowshape/dev` in pg_stat_activity during a pull — confirmed by querying the source database while one was running. Previously a DBA watching their primary saw an anonymous session running unfamiliar aggregates against their largest tables with nothing to attribute it to, which is a question that gets tools banned from production.

Three limits, set with SET LOCAL inside the read transaction so they last exactly as long as it and nothing is left behind on a pooled connection: statement_timeout (5m), lock_timeout (5s), idle_in_transaction_session_timeout (10m). Each is a flag, and a NEGATIVE value disables one — disabling has to be asked for, because a zero-valued struct field must not be a route to unlimited-against-production. lock_timeout is short on purpose: waiting is precisely the state in which `pull` blocks the queue behind a pending ALTER TABLE, and a lock that is not free in a few seconds is one worth backing off from.

The hard part was NOT setting the ceilings, it was making them degrade. A ceiling that ABORTS makes the tool unusable on exactly the large tables it is for: the operator lowers the limit to be safe and gets no fixture at all. First attempt did exactly that. So a profiling read that hits the ceiling now drops the fact it was computing, warns naming the column and `--statement-timeout`, and the run continues — an absent fact cannot license a PASS (§7.4), so a degraded fixture is conservative rather than wrong, and silent truncation stays forbidden.

That in turn exposed a second problem only the end-to-end run could find: a cancelled statement POISONS the read transaction, so the first degradation left every later statement failing with `current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block` — degrading one fact silently destroyed the rest of the pull. Each degradable read now runs inside its own savepoint, the same shape PR-T2 used on the load path. Per-read rather than per-table, so a timeout on one column's range does not cost the next column's. The structural catalog scan runs UNGUARDED and stays fatal: a catalog read that times out leaves nothing to describe, and the message now says so rather than leaving the operator with a bare SQLSTATE.

Eight reads route through the degrade path: range, histogram, text sample, bytea length, json shape, uniqueness probe, uniqueness escalation, and fan-out/orphan_fraction. Those are the expensive ones and every one of them is a fact the confidence model can do without.

Tests: three in internal/profile/limits_test.go. The degradation test seeds a 400,000-row table specifically so PROFILING it is measurably slower than reading its STRUCTURE — that gap is what makes it possible to time out the expensive reads while the cheap ones succeed, which is the situation the path exists for — then asserts a usable fixture comes back with all three columns intact and that every warning names both the column and the flag. The other two read `current_setting` inside a real read transaction to prove the three limits are actually in force rather than merely configurable, and that a negative value disables one while a zero does NOT.

Docs: the privacy page gained a "What `pull` does to the database it reads" section with the limits table, the degrade-not-abort rule, the application_name, and the read-only role requirement — the section an operator points at to get the tool approved.

tasks.title: A measured distinct count can exceed the row count
tasks.description: HyperLogLog at precision 14 has ~1.6% error in either direction, so on a high-cardinality column its estimate routinely lands above the row count. A fixture that says a column has more distinct values than the table has rows is internally incoherent, and any consumer computing selectivity as distinct/rows gets a ratio above 1 — which can flip an index-usefulness or fan-out judgement, and makes the fixture fail its own §3 readability goal. Clamp the reported estimate to the row count, keep `error` so the uncertainty is still visible, and do not silently upgrade the confidence: the value is still `measured`. Where distinct == rows and `unique` is absent, be careful not to imply uniqueness — INV-UNIQUENESS forbids inferring it from anything but an exact probe.

The `error` field and the `measured` confidence are unchanged by the clamp.
Clamping to equal the row count never causes `unique: true` to be inferred.
A property test over HLL output confirms the invariant across cardinalities that straddle the row count.

tasks.verified:
Verified against PostgreSQL 16.13: a real `pull` of the test schema now reports zero columns with `distinct` greater than `rows`. Before this, `app.events.id` came back as 41,305 distinct over 40,000 rows and `app.orders.customer_id` as 60,706 over 60,000.

HyperLogLog errs in BOTH directions (~1.6% at precision 14), so on a high-cardinality column its estimate routinely lands above the number of values there are. That is not merely imprecise, it is impossible: a consumer computing selectivity as distinct/rows gets a ratio above 1, which can flip an index-usefulness or fan-out judgement, and it makes the fixture fail its own §3 readability goal.

The clamp is against the number of values THE SKETCH ACTUALLY SAW, counted in the same loop that feeds it, rather than against the table's row count. That is the tighter bound (the query streams non-NULL values only) and it is correct for a mostly-null column, where the row count would be far too loose a ceiling. It costs one increment.

Deliberately NOT changed: `error` is kept and the confidence stays `measured`. The clamp removes an impossible reading; it does not turn an estimate into an exact count, and claiming otherwise would license a PASS this fact cannot support (§7.4). And `value == seen` does not imply uniqueness — INV-UNIQUENESS forbids inferring `unique` from anything but an exact probe, and nothing on this path writes it.

Tests: internal/profile/hll_clamp_test.go is DB-backed and seeds the case that provokes the overshoot — a fully distinct 40,000-row column, where the true cardinality sits exactly at the bound the estimate must not cross — plus a half-NULL column, which fails if the clamp uses the row count instead of the observed count. tasks.verified:
Verified with a real `rowshape pull`. A 200-table schema emits 246,129 bytes against RFC §3.3's stated "under 100KB" — 2.4× over, and nothing said so.

The claim survived because the only guard, TestEmitSizeUnder100KB, built its 200-table fixture BY HAND with facts deliberately "at estimated (bare)". It came in at 101,424 bytes against a 102,400 limit — 976 bytes of headroom, under 1% — and passed. That is the phase-dd pattern inside the test suite: a hand-authored fixture is self-consistent in ways a real one is not, so the guard defended a number no user would ever see. The margin was also thin enough that any addition to the emitted vocabulary — several of which this phase makes — would have turned it red for reasons unrelated to the change.

Which to move was decided by MEASURING where the bytes go across a real 200-table pull: range 16.1%, distinct 14.4%, unique 13.1%, inline confidence 11.5%, constraints 5.2%, indexes 4.5%, length 3.7%, format 2.5%. No single field dominates and there is no fat. Every one of the top four is load-bearing — `unique` and its confidence are the whole §7.2 story, `range` and `distinct` drive the findings — so slimming any of them costs information the format exists to carry, to defend a number that was never measured in the first place. Decision (D-021): CORRECT THE CLAIM. §3.3 now says under 320KB for a 200-table schema, about 1.2KB per table, which is what the emitter costs with room for the vocabulary to grow. The principle it serves is untouched: 320KB of YAML is still a file a reviewer reads in a diff. It is now a number derived from the artifact rather than asserted at it.

The guard is rebuilt from reality. TestEmitSizeAgainstBudget parses testdata/real-pull.yaml — the output of an actual `pull` against a 20-table schema shaped like §3.3's own description, a heavy tail of lookup tables plus a few wide ones — and asserts the PER-TABLE cost projected to 200 tables (1,083 bytes/table, 216,600 projected). Twenty tables so the testdata stays small; per-table because that is what actually drifts when the vocabulary grows. It also asserts a FLOOR, so the budget can never be quietly satisfied by the emitter LOSING facts — a sudden drop means fields stopped being written, not that anything got more efficient.

`pull` now warns at the moment it writes an over-budget fixture, naming what reduces it (`--schema`, or splitting the schema), because the failure mode otherwise is that nobody notices until a reviewer refuses the diff. `rowshape inspect --size` reports any fixture against the budget, comparing on per-table cost scaled to the quoted table count — otherwise a 10-table fixture would always look comfortable and a 500-table one always damning, regardless of how heavy the emitter had become.

A developer can pull a fixture without holding a production credential.
Registry downtime never breaks anyone's CI (fixtures still resolve from git).
verification: registry integration test: push/version/pull by id; access control enforced; git fallback works

tasks.title: Audit trail + approval gates
tasks.description: The compliance surface Priya writes the check for (PRD §8.4): an immutable audit trail of every validate — who, when, which fixture, what verdict — plus approval gates where a FAIL blocks the deploy and a WARN requires a named human override that is recorded. Never gate `validate` itself (PRD §8.4) — the moment validate is gated the agent loop breaks and the wedge dies.
spec_refs: PRD §8.4 (audit trail, approval gates; never gate validate)
acceptance_criteria: Every validate submitted to the cloud is recorded immutably (who/when/fixture/verdict).
Approval gates block a deploy on FAIL and require a recorded named override on WARN.
`validate` itself remains free and ungated — gating lives in the deploy gate, not the command.
verification: integration test: audit record immutable; FAIL blocks, WARN override recorded; validate never blocked

tasks.title: Drift detection (customer-side, signed results)
tasks.description: Scheduled `verify` against every environment, alerting when prod diverges from what the migration history claims (PRD §8.4). It MUST be customer-side (PRD §9): the customer runs a runner in their own infra that posts signed results — we never hold their production credentials, which would make us a breach target and kill the deal with the exact buyer we're chasing. The backend only receives and stores signed JSON.
spec_refs: PRD §9 (drift must be customer-side; receive and store signed JSON)
acceptance_criteria: A customer-side runner performs scheduled read-only `verify` and posts signed results.
The backend never holds production credentials — it only receives and stores signed JSON.
Divergence from the declared migration history raises an alert.
verification: integration test: signed verify result accepted and stored; unsigned/invalid rejected; no cred storage path exists

tasks.title: Agent attestation bound to CI workload identity
tasks.description: The differentiated feature (PRD §8.4): when an agent validated a migration, record which agent, which model, which fixture version, what verdict at the moment the PR opened. Self-reported identity is worthless — a `--agent=claude-code` flag is trivially spoofed — so attestation binds to a CI OIDC workload identity (GitHub Actions' token), signing verdict + fixture digest server-side. This makes attestation a CI product, not a laptop product; laptop validation stays useful and stays unattested.
spec_refs: PRD §8.4 (agent attestation; bind to CI OIDC, don't trust a flag)
PRD §9.1 (subject = fixture + migration digests; predicateType URI)
acceptance_criteria: Attestation binds to a CI OIDC workload identity, not a self-reported flag.
The signed predicate follows the PRD §9.1 shape (subject = fixture + migration digests, predicateType URI, verdict body as predicate).
Laptop validation is explicitly unattested and documented as such (the two are not blurred).
verification: integration test in CI: OIDC-bound attestation produced and verifies; spoofed flag alone yields no attestation

tasks.title: Attestation signing modes (Sigstore: public Rekor vs detached)
tasks.description: Resolve where signatures go (PRD §9.1 — decide in phase 5, not v1). Public Rekor makes immutability a property of the artifact, but keyless signing publishes repo identity + timing — free marketing for OSS, an unacceptable leak for a private enterprise monorepo. Ship two modes: public Rekor for OSS repos, and detached signatures held in the registry (or a private log) for enterprise. Don't be the root of trust — the artifact carries its own proof (PRD §9).
spec_refs: PRD §9.1 (two modes: public Rekor for OSS, detached/private for enterprise)
PRD §9 (don't be the root of trust)
acceptance_criteria: OSS mode publishes attestations to public Rekor, verifiable by anyone offline.
Enterprise mode uses detached signatures (registry or private log), leaking neither repo identity nor timing.
Verification works with zero trust in our server in both modes.
verification: test: OSS attestation verifies via Rekor; enterprise detached signature verifies offline without our server

tasks.title: Billing (Stripe) + pricing tiers — never gate validate
tasks.description: Wire billing per PRD §8.4/§9: Stripe, with the pricing shape ~$29/dev/mo or ~$99/connected-database/mo for registry + audit, enterprise for SSO/on-prem. The hard invariant: `validate` is free forever and never gated — the moment it's gated the agent loop breaks and the wedge dies (PRD §8.4). Cloud sells what only exists when there's more than one of you.
spec_refs: PRD §8.4 (pricing shape; never gate validate; MIT CLI, closed cloud)
acceptance_criteria: Stripe billing supports the per-dev and per-connected-database tiers plus an enterprise path.
`validate` (CLI + Action + MCP) remains free and ungated regardless of billing state.
The free CLI is complete on its own — a solo dev never hits a paywall (PRD §8.4).
verification: integration test: subscription lifecycle via Stripe test mode; validate works with no active subscription

milestones.note: Milestones map the PRD §14 sequence to shippable gates. The launch gate is the PRD §13 v1-done demo: a Claude Code session, given a repo and a fixture, told 'add a NOT NULL email column to users', produces a naive migration, watches it FAIL with RS-LOCK-001, rewrites it as a three-step backfill, and reaches PASS — with no human turn in between. Record it before writing the README.
milestones.launch_gate: PRD §13: the agent-loop demo closes with no human turn (naive migration -> FAIL RS-LOCK-001 -> three-step backfill -> PASS). That demo is the launch.

list.name: Foundation reserved, spec public, skeleton builds
list.definition: Namespaces + Go module path fixed; rowshape/fixture-spec public (RFC-0001 v1, MIT); single binary with stub subcommands; goreleaser signed + SBOM on five platforms; CI green.

list.name: pull + hydrate reproduce a corpus pathology (Week-6 gate)
list.definition: A read-only fast-mode `pull` emits a digest-stable <100KB fixture with confidence on every fact; `hydrate --seed N` deterministically reconstructs a disposable Postgres reproducing a known corpus pathology. The confidence engine (HLL, uniqueness probes, auto-escalation, inspect --leaks) is in.
list.kill_checkpoint: Week 6 (PRD §14.1): if pull + hydrate don't reproduce a known corpus pathology, the fixture premise is wrong — stop before building validate.

list.name: validate + verdict contract green; version-conditional model verified at its boundary
list.definition: Corpus + capping tests land before the findings; one Verdict struct with two marshalers (DSSE-signable); `validate` returns RS-LOCK / RS-DATA / RS-CONSTRAINT / RS-INDEX with bucketed, version-conditional estimates and mandatory remediation, capped by confidence (RFC §7.4). NOTE (D-015): the PG 11-17 CI matrix has never run — it needs the org from P0-T1. What IS verified is the version-conditional model at its only real boundary (PG 10 vs 11+, D-006/D-007), pinned by TestVersionConditionalBoundary against a live server. Real engine behavior on majors other than the one tested locally remains unobserved.

list.name: MCP server + init --agent wire the loop into the agent's turn
list.definition: `rowshape mcp` serves the four thin tools; `rowshape init --agent` writes MCP config, the versioned agent rule, and the pre-commit backstop so an agent reaches for rowshape unprompted.

list.name: Launch: agent-loop demo closes with no human turn (Week-12 gate)
list.definition: The wrong-verdict gaps found by the production deep dive are closed (phase-pr: a migration Postgres rejects never returns PASS, and a schema using extension types hydrates) and then the launch surfaces ship. GitHub Action runs `validate` in CI rendering the shared Verdict; docs site live on Cloudflare Pages with the narrow-and-true privacy claim; the agent-loop demo runs end-to-end (naive migration -> FAIL RS-LOCK-001 -> three-step backfill -> PASS) with no human turn, guarded by a CI regression job. This is v1-done and the launch.
list.kill_checkpoint: Week 12 (PRD §14.1): if the demo doesn't work end-to-end without a human turn, the wedge isn't real — reassess.

list.name: Post-launch traction gate (Week-20) unlocks cloud
list.definition: Findings breadth (RS-PERF, RS-REVERSE), version-matrix depth, and MySQL proceed ungated. The cloud (registry, audit, drift, attestation, billing) is built only if the traction gate passes; `validate` is never gated.
list.kill_checkpoint: Week 20 (PRD §14.1): zero unsolicited issues/PRs is information, not a reason to push harder — cloud does not start without organic pull-through.

open_decisions.status_note: DECIDED BY OMISSION, NOT BY CHOICE — needs an explicit call. The recorded leaning is 'capture, don't act', but pg_stat_statements appears NOWHERE in the codebase, so the opposite was shipped without anyone deciding it. Its resolve_by (phase-1 / P1-T1) has passed. Either accept 'omit entirely' deliberately, or implement the leaning — but the fixture schema is now stable, which is exactly the retrofit cost the question warned about.
open_decisions.question: Capture pg_stat_statements in v1 fixtures without acting on it, or omit it entirely?
open_decisions.leaning: Capture, don't act (schema-additive; decide early because retrofitting the fixture schema is costly).

open_decisions.leaning: Unresolved — decides how frictionless the agent loop feels on first run; couples to the exit-3 tool-error path (P2-T17).

open_decisions.leaning: Parent declares partitions: {count, strategy, skew}; no per-partition entries (implemented in P1-T12).
